facts.statement: The genus Hyposaurus was first described by Richard Owen in 1849.
facts.quote: authority: Owen, 1849

facts.statement: Hyposaurus is an extinct marine crocodyliform belonging to the family Dyrosauridae.
facts.quote: Hyposaurus is a genus of extinct marine dyrosaurid crocodyliform.

facts.statement: Fossils of Hyposaurus have been found in rocks dating from the Late Cretaceous to the Early Paleocene in West Africa, Sudan, and the eastern United States.
facts.quote: Fossils have been found in Paleocene aged rocks of the Iullemmeden Basin in West Africa, Campanian–Maastrichtian (Late Cretaceous) Shendi Formation of Sudan and Maastrichtian (Late Cretaceous) through Danian (Early Paleocene) strata in New Jersey, Alabama and South Carolina.

facts.statement: Hyposaurus is classified as a mesosuchian crocodyliform within the family Dyrosauridae.
facts.quote: It is a mesosuchian crocodyliform in the family Dyrosauridae.

facts.statement: Hyposaurus is closely related to the genera Dyrosaurus and Congosaurus.
facts.quote: It is closely related to dyrosaurs and congosaurs

facts.statement: Hyposaurus lived in shallow, near-shore marine environments and possessed many aquatic adaptations.
facts.quote: Hyposaurus lived in a shallow, near shore marine environment and has many aquatic adaptations

facts.statement: The first fossil recognized by Owen in 1849 consisted of two amphicoelous vertebrae discovered by Professor Henry Roger.
facts.quote: Owen first recognized the genus in 1849. This first fossil was two amphicoelous vertebrae, vertebrae with two concave sides of the centrum, discovered by Professor Henry Roger.

facts.statement: The initial fossils were found in the greensand beds of New Jersey, now the location of the Edelman Fossil Park and Museum.
facts.quote: It was found in the greensand beds in New Jersey, currently the site of the Edelman Fossil Park and Museum.

facts.statement: The genus name Hyposaurus refers to a unique hypapophyseal keel extending on the ventral surface of the vertebrae.
facts.quote: The genus name is meant to describe the unique "hypapophyseal keel extended on the ventral surface of the centrum".

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope found a second fossil in Brazil in 1886, which included a lower jaw, vertebrae, and various other bones.
facts.quote: The second fossil find was by Cope in 1886. This fossil was found in Brazil and comprises a left molar, quadratojugal bone, a lower jaw, many vertebrae from the middle to posterior parts of the column, a humerus, a coracoid bone, teeth, and several other bones.

facts.statement: Hyposaurus differs from Teleosaurus by having teeth with a more robust size and vertical orientation.
facts.quote: The differences between Hyposaurus and Teleosaurus are described as "the robust size and vertical direction" of the teeth of Hyposaurus

facts.statement: The dorsal shield of Hyposaurus consists of at least 12 horizontal rows of paravertebral and accessory osteoderms.
facts.quote: The dorsal shield is made of two columns of paravertebral osteoderms and two lateral columns of accessory osteoderms. At least 12 horizontal rows of these make up the shield.

facts.statement: Hyposaurus differs from modern crocodiles by having tall neural spines, vertically oriented ribs, and keel-less osteoderms.
facts.quote: The three main differences between the axial skeletons of Hyposaurus and modern crocodylians are the tall neural spines, vertically oriented thoracic ribs and osteoderm which lack external keels.

facts.statement: Specialized osteoderms suggest Hyposaurus had a trunk bracing system that allowed low-mass individuals to high-walk or gallop.
facts.quote: Along with the specialized osteoderm morphology, Hyposaurus probably had a specialized trunk bracing system which suggests that individuals with low body mass could have only high walked or galloped.

facts.statement: Hyposaurus had a long tail, eyes positioned on the sides of its head, and a long snout with many uniform teeth.
facts.quote: In addition, its tail was long, both eyes were on the side of the head, and the snout was long with many uniform teeth.

facts.statement: Short transverse processes on the tail vertebrae imply that Hyposaurus did not move its tail vertically and was likely not a diving animal.
facts.quote: The short transverse process on the caudal vertebrae implies the tail did not move vertically, indicating that Hyposaurus was not a diving animal.

facts.statement: The phylogeny of Hyposaurus is disputed, with some researchers suggesting it is a sister taxon to Dyrosaurids, Congosaurus, and Acherontisuchus.
facts.quote: There is a disputed phylogeny with many interpretations. Some paleontologists interpret that Dyrosaurids, Congosaurus, and Acherontisuchus are sister taxa of Hyposaurus.

facts.statement: The genus Hyposaurus was named by Richard Owen in 1849.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Owen, 1849

facts.statement: Hyposaurus belongs to the crocodyliform family Dyrosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Dyrosauridae

facts.statement: The dorsal shield of Hyposaurus consisted of four columns of osteoderms: two paravertebral and two lateral.
facts.quote: The dorsal shield is made of two columns of paravertebral osteoderms and two lateral columns of accessory osteoderms.

facts.statement: The dorsal shield of Hyposaurus was composed of at least 12 horizontal rows of osteoderms.
facts.quote: At least 12 horizontal rows of these make up the shield.

facts.statement: The vertebrae of Hyposaurus are weakly amphicoelous, with concave centers on both sides.
facts.quote: The vertebrae are weakly amphicoelous, meaning both sides of the centrum are concave.

facts.statement: Hyposaurus is an extinct genus of dyrosaurid crocodyliform.
facts.quote: Hyposaurus es un género extinto de crocodilomorfo dirosáurido.

facts.statement: Fossils of Hyposaurus have been found in the Paleocene Maria Farinha Formation in Brazil, the Iullemmeden Basin in West Africa, and Maastrichtian strata in New Jersey, USA.
facts.quote: Sus fósiles han sido encontrados en rocas que datan del Paleoceno de la Formación Maria Farinha en Pernambuco, Brasil y la Cuenca Iullemmeden en el África Occidental y estratos del Maastrichtiense (Cretácico Superior) en Nueva Jersey, Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: The type species H. rogersii was described by Richard Owen in 1849 based on Late Cretaceous fossils from North America.
facts.quote: La especie tipo, H. rogersii, fue descrita en 1849 por Richard Owen sobre la base de fósiles del Cretácico Superior de América del Norte.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope described the species H. derbianus in 1886 based on fossils found in Brazil.
facts.quote: En 1886, Edward Drinker Cope describió la especie H. derbianus sobre la base de fósiles encontrados en Brasil.

facts.statement: Swinton described two species from Paleocene deposits in Nigeria in 1930, classifying them as the genera Sokotosaurus and Wurnosaurus.
facts.quote: En 1930, Swinton describió dos especies de los depósitos paleocenos de Nigeria —H. nopcsai y H. wilsoni—, clasificándolos en dos géneros, Sokotosaurus y Wurnosaurus, respectivamente.

facts.statement: Schwarz and colleagues described new postcranial skeletons of Hyposaurus in 2006, focusing primarily on the vertebrae.
facts.quote: In 2006 Schwarz and colleagues, described the postcranial skeletons of new specimens of Hyposaurus, focusing mostly on the vertebrae.

facts.statement: It is debated whether H. wilsoni and H. nopcsai are distinct species, as their little variation suggests one might be a nomen dubium despite fossil evidence for two.
facts.quote: The little variation between the species Hyposaurus wilsoni and Hyposaurus nopcsai, means one of the two is a nomen dubium (Latin: "doubtful name"), although fossil evidence does suggest two species.

facts.statement: The weakly amphicoelous nature of Hyposaurus vertebrae indicates both sides of the centrum are concave.
facts.quote: The vertebrae are weakly amphicoelous, meaning both sides of the centrum are concave.

facts.statement: Hyposaurus lived from the Maastrichtian to the Thanetian, approximately 72.2 to 56 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Thanetian (72.2 to 56 million years ago)

facts.statement: In 2007, Stéphane Jouve considered Sokotosaurus and Wurnosaurus as doubtful genera indistinguishable from each other and North American forms.
facts.quote: En 2007, ambos fueron considerados por Stéphane Jouve como géneros dudosos, indistinguibles unos de otros, así como las formas de América del Norte.

facts.statement: Hastings and colleagues used mandibular and cranial characteristics to map a new dyrosaurid skull from Colombia onto a cladogram including Hyposaurus.
facts.quote: A paper by Hastings and colleagues described a new skull of a dyrosaurid crocodyliform, found in the Cerrejón Formation of northern Colombia. They used mandibular and cranial characteristics to map it onto a cladogram with Hyposaurus and other taxa.

facts.statement: Analysis suggests Dyrosauridae originated in Africa and dispersed to South America in the Late Cretaceous or very early Paleocene.
facts.quote: Analysis supports an African origin to Dyrosauridae, with dispersal and radiation in South America in the Late Cretaceous or very early Paleocene.

facts.statement: Hyposaurus rogersii is a contender for the second smallest species in the family Dyrosauridae.
facts.quote: This specimen of dyrosaurid is the smallest of the family Dyrosauridae found to date, with Hyposaurus rogersii being a contender for the next smallest.

facts.statement: A Sudanese fossil was identified as Hyposaurus based on its flat mandible and elliptical mandibular symphysis.
facts.quote: It was identified as a Hyposaurus based on the flat shape of the mandible (lower jawbone) and the elliptical shape of the mandibular symphysis (median line ridge of mandible).

facts.statement: Six species are currently recognized within the genus Hyposaurus: H. derbianus, H. natator, H. nopcsai, H. paucidens, H. rogersii, and H. wilsoni.
facts.quote: subdivision: H. derbianus Cope, 1886 H. natator Troxell, 1925 H. nopcsai (Swinton, 1930) H. paucidens Arambourg, 1952 H. rogersii Owen, 1849 H. wilsoni (Swinton, 1930)
